pll1d19c4-d1e3477.summary: States that hence the Father is said to be in the Son, the Son in the Father, the Spirit in both, and each in each.
claims: The persons are in one another.

pll1d19c4-d1e3480.summary: Cites the De fide ad Petrum: by natural unity the whole Father is in the Son and Spirit, and the whole Spirit in Father and Son; none is outside another. This partly explains, as far as the mystery can be opened by man, how each is wholly in the others.
claims: By unity of nature each person is wholly in the others.
None is outside another.
The mystery cannot be fully opened by humans.

pll1d19c4-d1e3503.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate III: 'I in the Father and the Father in me' is obscure because human reason cannot grasp it and no human comparison fits, yet what is unintelligible to man is possible to God. The fullness of divinity is in both: what is in the Unbegotten is in the Begotten, one from the other and both one, 'not two one, but one in the other, because not another thing in both.' The Son received all; had he received a part, neither would be perfect.
claims: Human understanding cannot grasp the mutual indwelling.
The fullness of divinity is in both Father and Son.
Father and Son are one in the other, without another thing in both.
The Son received the whole, not a part, of the Father.

pll1d19c4-d1e3616.summary: Further Hilary, De Trinitate VII: the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, God in God, not by joining two kinds or by one substance containing another, but by the united likeness of nature, through the birth of living nature from living nature, with nothing new, alien, or separable.
claims: The indwelling is not by composition or containment.
It is by united likeness of nature through birth.
Nothing new, alien, or separable is in the divine birth.

pll1d19c4-d1e3638.summary: Draws out the sense: as far as human weakness allows, Christ is in the Father and the Father in him, and so too the Spirit in both and each in each, because the same fullness of divinity and united likeness of nature is in each, the nature being no greater in any person.
claims: Each person is in the others because each has the same fullness of divinity.
The divine nature is no greater in any person.

pll1d19c4-d1e3641.summary: Cites Ambrose on 2 Corinthians: the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father because their substance is one, for there is unity where there is no diversity.
claims: Father and Son are in each other because their substance is one.

pll1d19c4-d1e3660.summary: Notes that the three witnesses, Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose, agree by revelation of the Spirit speaking in them, showing to those willing to believe, though as in a mirror and in an enigma, how the persons are in one another.
claims: Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose agree on mutual indwelling.
This is understood only as in a mirror, in an enigma.

pll1d19c4-d1e3681.summary: Returns to the thesis: no person exceeds another in magnitude, nor two one, nor three two, nor God all of them, since each is perfect and that perfection cannot grow.
claims: No person exceeds another in magnitude.
Each person is perfect and cannot be increased.

pl-l1d19c4.summary: Explains that, because the whole essence is in each, the persons are said to be in one another (John 14:11). Augustine: by natural unity the whole Father is in the Son and Spirit, and none is outside another. Hilary acknowledges that this exceeds human understanding: the fullness of divinity is in both, what is in the Unbegotten is in the Begotten, 'not two one, but one in the other, because not another thing in both.' The Son received all, not a part, and Father and Son are in each other by the united likeness of nature through the birth of living nature from living nature. Ambrose: Father and Son are in each other because their substance is one. These three witnesses show 'as in a mirror' how the persons are in one another. Lombard returns to the thesis: none exceeds another in magnitude, since each is perfect.
claims: The persons are in one another: the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, the Spirit in both.
Mutual indwelling follows from the unity of the divine nature.
The fullness of divinity is in each person.
The Son received the whole, not a part, of the Father's nature.
Father and Son are in each other through the united likeness of nature, not by composition.
The mutual indwelling exceeds human understanding and is grasped as in a mirror.
No person exceeds another in magnitude, since each is perfect.
